How to Lower Blood Pressure Naturally: 10 Little Wins That Help

12 min read · October 2026 · Little Wins Health

What's in this guide

  • Can small changes lower blood pressure?
  • How much each change helps
  • 10 natural ways to lower blood pressure
  • Checking your blood pressure at home
  • Lifestyle changes and medication
  • When to see a doctor
  • Your one little win
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Sources

The cuff tightens, slowly lets go, and the number on the screen is higher than you expected. Maybe it's 134/86, or maybe it's the second high reading this year. Your doctor mentions "lifestyle changes," and it can sound like you're being asked to rebuild your whole life by Monday.

You aren't. Learning how to lower blood pressure naturally comes down to small, everyday changes, each one bringing your numbers down a few points. Put a few of them together and the drop can reach 10 points or more on the top number.

Each of the 10 little wins below comes with how much it helps and how to fit it into a normal day.

Key Takeaways

  • Healthy habits are the first treatment the latest US guideline recommends for raised blood pressure, and they still help if you take medication.
  • Small changes stack. Cutting salt, moving more and eating more potassium-rich food each lower the top number by a few points.
  • People with higher readings generally see the biggest drops.
  • Never stop or change your blood pressure medication without talking to your doctor first.

Can Small Changes Really Lower Blood Pressure?

Yes. The 2025 high blood pressure guideline from the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology puts healthy habits at the center of treatment for everyone with raised blood pressure. It also asks doctors to work with patients on realistic, achievable goals, which is exactly what little wins are.

Each habit works on your blood pressure in a slightly different way. For example, eating less salt means your body holds on to less water, so there's less fluid pressing against your artery walls. Moving more helps your blood vessels relax and widen, and losing extra weight eases the load on your heart.

Because they work in different ways, the benefits build on each other. Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against your artery walls each time your heart beats, so anything that lowers the amount of fluid, relaxes the vessels or lightens your heart's workload brings that force down. That's why a few small changes, each working on a different part of the system, can move your numbers.

Time also plays a part. For people with stage 1 high blood pressure (130 to 139 over 80 to 89) and a lower risk of heart disease, the guideline recommends trying lifestyle changes for 3 to 6 months before starting medication. That gives your little wins a fair chance to show up in your readings.

How Much Do Lifestyle Changes Lower Blood Pressure?

Most single changes lower the top number, called systolic pressure, by about 3 to 8 points in people with high blood pressure. Those figures come from a 2025 review of lifestyle treatment for high blood pressure in primary care, which drew on the latest US guideline. Bigger changes, like following the DASH eating plan fully, can do more.

How much each change can lower the top number
ChangeRough drop in the top number
Losing weightAbout 1 point for every 1 kg (2.2 lb) lost
Following the DASH eating plan1 to 13 points
Cutting salt from a typical high intakeAbout 7 points
Eating more potassiumAbout 6 points
Using a potassium salt substituteAbout 3 to 5 points
Aerobic exercise, like brisk walkingAbout 4 to 7 points
Resistance training, like weightsAbout 3 points
Isometric exercise, like wall sitsAbout 8 points
Cutting heavy drinking by half or moreA noticeable drop

Your own result may be bigger or smaller than these averages. People with higher readings tend to see larger drops. The salt figures show this well, with about 3 points for people with normal readings and about 7 for those with high blood pressure.

The effects don't add up perfectly, so two 5-point changes won't always give you 10. Two or three changes together generally do more than any one alone, though, and that's where the real progress comes from.

10 Natural Ways to Lower Blood Pressure

None of these asks you to change everything at once. Pick one or two that fit your life right now, give them a few weeks, and add another once they feel normal.

1. Swap 5 Minutes of Sitting for Brisk Movement

Five minutes is enough to start. In a study of 14,761 adults across five countries, swapping just 5 minutes of less active time each day for activities like running, cycling or climbing stairs lowered the top number by 0.68 points and the bottom number by 0.54 points.

That sounds small, but the benefit grows with time spent. About 20 extra minutes a day of that kind of activity lowered the top number by 2 points, enough for researchers to call it clinically meaningful.

You don't need a gym for this. Take the stairs at work, walk briskly to the shops, or try a 10-minute walk after dinner, which also helps keep blood sugar in check. Choose a pace that leaves you a little breathless but still able to talk.

2. Sit 30 Minutes Less Each Day

Cutting sitting time works even when you aren't exercising. In a 6-month trial of 283 adults aged 60 to 89, people who sat about 30 minutes less each day than the comparison group saw their top number fall by 3.48 points more.

The people in that trial used a standing desk, a fitness tracker that buzzed to remind them to get up, and regular check-ins with a coach. You can copy the idea for free. Stand while you're on phone calls, get up during TV ad breaks, or set a phone reminder to stand and stretch every half hour.

3. Use a Potassium Salt Substitute at Home

A potassium salt substitute replaces some of the sodium in regular salt with potassium, so food still tastes salty. The 2025 US guideline now lists potassium-based salt substitutes as a way to prevent and treat high blood pressure, especially for people who add most of their salt while cooking at home.

The evidence behind it is large. The Salt Substitute and Stroke Study followed 20,995 people in 600 rural Chinese villages who had either had a stroke or were over 60 with high blood pressure. Villages that switched to a salt made of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride had fewer strokes, fewer heart attacks and fewer deaths than villages that kept using regular salt.

This swap isn't safe for everyone. People with kidney disease, and those taking potassium supplements or certain blood pressure drugs like ACE inhibitors, can build up too much potassium. Check with your doctor or pharmacist before you switch.

4. Cut the Salt Hiding in Everyday Foods

Most of the salt you eat never comes from your salt shaker. A CDC analysis of US eating habits found that about 65% of sodium comes from food bought in stores and about 25% from restaurants. Bread and rolls were the biggest single source, followed by cold cuts and cured meats, pizza and soup.

The 2025 guideline sets a limit of 2,300 mg of sodium a day, with 1,500 mg as the ideal, and many adults eat far more. A few swaps bring that down without making meals bland. Compare bread labels and pick the lower-sodium loaf, use fresh chicken in sandwiches instead of deli meat, and season with garlic, lemon, herbs or pepper before you reach for salt or stock cubes.

Reading labels gets quicker with practice. Check the sodium per serving, and use the FDA's guide to the percent daily value on food labels, which counts 5% or less as low and 20% or more as high.

5. Add Potassium-Rich Foods to Your Plate

Potassium is the counterweight to salt. The American Heart Association explains that the more potassium you eat, the more sodium your body flushes out in urine, and potassium also helps relax blood vessel walls. Adults aged 19 to 50 need about 3,400 mg a day for men and 2,600 mg for women.

Good sources include bananas, sweet potatoes, potatoes, avocados, spinach, tomatoes, beans, oranges, melons, yogurt and fish. These foods sit at the heart of the DASH eating plan, but you can start small. Add beans to a stew, keep bananas or oranges on the counter, or swap chips for a baked sweet potato.

Food is the safest way to get more potassium. The same kidney and medication cautions apply here, and you should talk to your doctor before taking potassium supplements.

6. Try Wall Sits and Plank Holds

Holding still can lower blood pressure more than you'd expect. In a review of 270 trials with nearly 16,000 people, isometric exercise, where your muscles work without moving, lowered the top number by about 8 points. That was almost twice the drop seen with aerobic exercise or weight training in the same review.

Wall sits did best of all, though only four trials tested them. To try one, lean your back against a wall and slide down until your knees are bent, as if you're sitting on an invisible chair. The trials generally used 4 holds of 2 minutes each, with 1 to 4 minutes of rest between them, three times a week.

Start with shorter holds and work up. Breathe normally the whole time, because holding your breath can push your blood pressure up for a moment. If your readings are very high, ask your doctor before you start.

7. Drink Less Alcohol

The 2025 guideline now says the ideal amount of alcohol is none. For people who do drink, it sets a limit of no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women.

Cutting back helps most if you drink more than that. In a review of 36 trials with 2,865 adults, people who had more than two drinks a day lowered their blood pressure when they drank less. Those who had six or more a day and cut their intake by about half saw the top number fall by 5.5 points.

Small swaps make cutting back easier. Alternate each drink with a glass of water, choose smaller glasses, or plan two or three alcohol-free days each week.

8. Lose a Little Weight If You Need To

You don't have to reach a goal weight to see a difference. A review of 25 trials with 4,874 people found the top number fell by about 1 point for every kilogram (2.2 lb) lost. People in those trials lost about 5 kg (11 lb) on average and lowered the top number by about 4.4 points.

The 2025 guideline suggests a first goal of losing at least 5% of your body weight if you have overweight or obesity. For someone who weighs 90 kg (198 lb), that's about 4.5 kg (10 lb).

The other wins on this list can help you get there, especially moving more and eating less processed food.

9. Protect Your Sleep

Sleep gives your heart and blood vessels time to recover. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute warns that going short on sleep over a long period raises your risk of high blood pressure, and it recommends 7 to 9 hours a night for adults.

Small habits make good sleep easier. Go to bed and wake up at the same time each day, avoid caffeine later in the day, and keep alcohol and heavy meals away from bedtime. A cool, dark, quiet bedroom helps too.

If you snore loudly, wake up gasping or still feel tired after a full night in bed, talk to your doctor. These can be signs of a sleep problem that needs treatment.

10. Give Stress a Daily Outlet

Stress raises your blood pressure for a while, and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute notes that long-term stress can contribute to high blood pressure. It can also push you toward habits that raise it further, like drinking more, smoking or eating more salty comfort food.

You can't remove every source of stress, but you can give it somewhere to go. Physical activity, meditation, relaxation exercises and talking with friends or family all help. A few minutes of slow breathing before bed, or a short walk at lunch, is a good place to start.

Living with a long-term health condition can add its own worries. If stress or low mood starts to weigh on you, there's more on looking after your mental health with a long-term condition, and a counselor can also help.

How to Check Your Blood Pressure at Home and Track Your Little Wins

Home readings show you if your little wins are working. One reading at the clinic is a snapshot, while a week of readings at home shows your real pattern, and the 2025 guideline recommends home monitoring to confirm a diagnosis and track progress.

How you take a reading changes the number you see. The American Heart Association's home monitoring advice covers these basics.

  • Skip caffeine, smoking and exercise for 30 minutes before you measure, and empty your bladder.
  • Sit quietly for 5 minutes in a chair with your back supported, feet flat on the floor and legs uncrossed.
  • Rest your arm on a table so your upper arm sits at heart level, and put the cuff on bare skin just above the bend of your elbow.
  • Take two readings one minute apart, at the same times each day, such as morning and evening.
  • Write both numbers down, or let your monitor store them, and bring them to your appointments.

Choose an automatic monitor with an upper-arm cuff, since wrist and finger monitors are less reliable. Check that it's been tested for accuracy on the US list of validated blood pressure monitors at validatebp.org, and bring it to your doctor once a year so they can compare it with their equipment.

High blood pressure and high blood sugar often show up together, so your doctor may check both. If you've been told your blood sugar is raised too, it helps to understand how type 2 diabetes develops.

Lifestyle Changes and Blood Pressure Medication

Little wins work alongside blood pressure medication; they don't replace it. If your doctor has prescribed tablets, keep taking them while you build new habits.

Lifestyle changes still help people who need several medicines. In the TRIUMPH trial of 140 adults already taking at least three blood pressure drugs, a 4-month program of exercise, weight loss, the DASH eating plan and less salt left the top number about 6 points lower than in a group that only got advice.

As your habits change, your readings may drop enough that your doctor lowers your dose. That decision belongs to your doctor, though. Never stop or cut back your medication on your own, even if your home readings look good.

When to See a Doctor About High Blood Pressure

See your doctor if your home readings sit at 130/80 or higher on most days, which counts as stage 1 high blood pressure, or if they keep climbing despite the changes you've made. Book a visit too if you get new headaches, dizziness or side effects from your medication.

A reading above 180/120 needs fast action. The American Heart Association's advice on when to call 911 is to wait at least a minute and measure again. If it's still that high and you feel fine, contact your doctor the same day.

Call emergency services straight away if a reading above 180/120 comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness or weakness, changes in your vision or difficulty speaking. Don't wait to see if it comes down on its own.

Your One Little Win

One little win

Tonight, swap 5 minutes on the couch for a brisk walk around the block or a few trips up and down the stairs. It's a small start, and it's one your blood pressure will notice.

Frequently Asked Questions About Lowering Blood Pressure

How Quickly Can Lifestyle Changes Lower Blood Pressure?

Many people see changes within a few months. The 2025 guideline gives people with stage 1 high blood pressure 3 to 6 months of lifestyle changes before deciding on medication, and the TRIUMPH program lowered readings within 4 months. Checking at home every day helps you spot progress early.

Can You Lower Blood Pressure Without Medication?

Some people can, especially those with elevated or stage 1 readings. Cutting salt, moving more, eating more potassium-rich food, losing extra weight and drinking less alcohol can together lower the top number by 10 points or more. If your readings stay high, medication protects your heart, brain and kidneys while your habits catch up.

Does Walking Lower Blood Pressure Right Away?

Every bit of brisk movement helps, but the lasting benefit comes from doing it most days. In the five-country study, swapping just 5 minutes of sitting for brisk activity lowered the top number slightly, and about 20 extra minutes a day lowered it by 2 points.

Is a Salt Substitute Safe for Everyone?

No. Potassium salt substitutes can raise potassium to unsafe levels in people with kidney disease and in those taking potassium supplements or certain blood pressure drugs, such as ACE inhibitors. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before you switch.

How Much Does Losing Weight Lower Blood Pressure?

On average, the top number drops by about 1 point for every kilogram (2.2 lb) you lose. Losing 5 kg (11 lb) brought the top number down by about 4.4 points in trials, and the guideline suggests aiming for at least 5% of your body weight as a first goal.
